analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers sell individual policies nationwide under the rules of whichever state they choose.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in December 2007, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let a health insurer pick one state — likely the one with the fewest rules — as its 'primary state' and sell individual health insurance policies in every other state under that state's laws, overriding the consumer protections, mandated benefits, and rate rules of the states where the buyers live. Supporters said this would make coverage cheaper by letting insurers avoid 50 different sets of state rules. The bill included some guardrails — a disclosure notice, an outside appeals process for denied claims, and limits on raising premiums based on health status at renewal — but it would have stripped states of most of their authority over policies sold to their own residents.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers gain the most: they could designate a lightly regulated state as their governing law and sell stripped-down, cheaper policies nationwide, free of other states' mandated benefits and premium rules. Healthy people in heavily regulated states might find cheaper bare-bones coverage. The bill's own required disclosure tells buyers a policy 'may be less expensive... because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state [S3].

how_it_helps.text: An insurer could designate one state as its 'primary state' and sell individual policies in every other state exempt from those states' insurance laws, except for limited rules the bill preserved: taxes, financial solvency examinations, fraud and abuse laws, unfair claims settlement practices, and an independent external review of denied claims [S3].
The bill's stated purpose was to make individual coverage more affordable by removing what it called the impediment of 'numerous and significant variations in State law' [S3].

It included some buyer protections: insurers could not reclassify an individual or raise that person's premium at renewal based on health status [S3], policies sold across state lines required a bold-type notice telling buyers the policy is not subject to all of their own state's coverage mandates and consumer protections [S3], and issuers could not sell into a secondary state unless their primary state used a risk-based capital formula for solvency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions and residents of states with strong consumer protections. Cheaper policies would cover less — the bill's own notice says so [S3] — and healthier buyers drawn to those policies would leave state insurance pools smaller and sicker, pushing up costs for those who stayed. State insurance regulators would lose most of their authority over policies sold to their residents, since the primary state would have sole power to enforce the governing laws [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's own mandated disclosure warns buyers that cheaper policies 'may be less expensive... because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state, 'including coverage of some services or benefits mandated by' state law, and are 'not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' [S3].

Because the primary state has sole jurisdiction to enforce the governing laws, a resident of a secondary state who is wronged would depend on another state's regulator and courts applying that other state's laws [S3].

The bill required the Comptroller General to study whether the change would affect the number of uninsured, the availability and cost of coverage for people with pre-existing conditions, the elimination of benefits, and cases of fraud — an acknowledgment that supporters could not promise the outcome [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings for healthy buyers would be real but would come from thinner coverage: fewer mandated benefits, weaker consumer protections, and rate rules of whichever state the insurer picked. The people most likely to lose are those with pre-existing conditions, who would remain in state pools shrinking as healthier buyers defect — the very outcome the bill's own GAO study provision was designed to measure. The bill's external review and renewal protections soften this, but do not replace the state laws it overrides.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced late in the session and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shadegg introduced the bill on December 12, 2007, with 63 Republican cosponsors; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Health [S1][S5].
The action history records no further action — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators, and people with pre-existing conditions in states with guaranteed-issue and strong consumer-protection rules, kept the protections the bill would have overridden. Health insurers did not get the ability to charter in the least-regulated state and sell nationwide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and protected insurance buyers

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 63 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it stayed in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 63 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would let an insurer choose the least-regulated state as its governing law and sell bare-bones policies nationwide, dodging other states' mandated benefits and rate rules — the bill's own disclosure notice tells buyers the policy skips those protections. Its gains come at the cost of coverage protections for the people buying the policies.

industries.industry: State insurance regulators and state consumer-protection regimes
industries.note: The bill exempts issuers from secondary states' insurance laws and gives the primary state sole enforcement power, stripping states of authority over policies sold to their own residents. Their loss in this bill runs alongside ordinary people's loss of state protections.
